performers: Hans Duhan, baritone; Ferdinand Foll, piano
intro: A man leaves his lover’s house in snow, keeping step with the piano. In Hans Duhan’s Gute Nacht, the first verse leads straight to the third; the final verse turns briefly to major as he closes the door quietly.

sections.label: Intro · Six bars of walking chords
sections.mNote: Repeated piano quavers establish a steady pace

sections.label: A · A stranger arrives and leaves
sections.mNote: The voice descends over the piano’s continuing steps

sections.label: B · Love wanders from one to another
sections.mNote: The third verse follows the first in this recording

sections.label: C · A quiet goodnight in the major
sections.mNote: The piano keeps walking as the harmony brightens

sections.label: Coda · The piano walks on in the minor
sections.mNote: A tempo restores the pace for the last piano bars

cues.title: Six bars of footsteps
cues.text: Mässig, in gehender Bewegung — moderate, with a walking motion. The piano sets off in repeated quaver chords before the voice arrives. The tread is already there; the singer has to join it.
cues.evidence: OpenScore Lieder, bars 1–7: opening marking, repeated quavers and vocal pickup in bar 7. https://musescore.com/openscore-lieder-corpus/scores/5015378
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A stranger at both ends
cues.text: “Fremd bin ich eingezogen, / Fremd zieh’ ich wieder aus.” I came here a stranger; a stranger I leave. Müller puts the same word at the start of both lines. Schubert’s melody falls over the piano’s steady steps.
cues.evidence: Wilhelm Müller, Gute Nacht, opening couplet, in Die Winterreise (1824); our translation of the German at https://oxfordsong.org/song/gute-nacht. OpenScore Lieder, bars 7–14: https://musescore.com/openscore-lieder-corpus/scores/5015378.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Love has wandering feet
cues.text: Duhan goes straight to the third verse, leaving out the second. “Die Liebe liebt das Wandern” — love loves to wander. The singer gives love the same restless feet that carry him away from the house.
cues.evidence: Christian Utz, ZGMTH 18 (2021), footnote 25, documents Duhan and Foll’s omitted second stanza: https://www.gmth.de/zeitschrift/artikel/1132.aspx. Wilhelm Müller, Gute Nacht, third stanza, in Die Winterreise (1824); our translation: https://oxfordsong.org/song/gute-nacht. OpenScore, bar 39 onward: https://musescore.com/openscore-lieder-corpus/scores/5015378.

cues.title: A cycle of horrifying songs
cues.text: Joseph von Spaun recalls Schubert’s invitation: “Come to Schober’s today, I’ll sing you a cycle of horrifying songs.” Schubert then sings the whole of Winterreise in an emotional voice, and his friends are dumbfounded by its sombre mood.
cues.evidence: Joseph von Spaun’s recollection, quoted in Heinrich Welti’s article on Schubert, Allgemeine Deutsche Biographie 32 (1891), p. 626: “Komm heute zu Schober, ich werde Euch einen Cyclus schauerlicher Lieder vorsingen … Wir waren durch die düstere Stimmung dieser Lieder ganz verblüfft”. Translation ours. https://de.wikisource.org/wiki/ADB:Schubert,_Franz_(Komponist)

cues.title: The door closes softly
cues.text: The last verse turns to the major. He does not want to wake her, so he closes the door softly and writes goodnight on the gate. The piano keeps the same walking chords beneath this unexpectedly tender farewell.
cues.evidence: Müller, Gute Nacht, fourth stanza: https://oxfordsong.org/song/gute-nacht. OpenScore Lieder, bar 71 onward: original D minor changes to D major, with the accompaniment continuing in quavers. https://musescore.com/openscore-lieder-corpus/scores/5015378
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The first complete recording
cues.text: Hans Duhan’s Winterreise is the earliest complete recording, made for HMV in 1928, the centenary of Schubert’s death. He records nineteen songs with Ferdinand Foll on 27 April, 2 May and 4 May, and the other five with Lene Orthmann in July.
cues.evidence: Christian Utz, “Exzentrisch geformte Klang-Landschaften”, ZGMTH 18 (2021), section 2: nineteen songs with Foll on 27 April, 2 May and 4 May 1928, the remaining five (Nos. 16, 17, 19, 20, 23) with Lene Orthmann on 11 July 1928, for HMV in the centenary year of Schubert’s death. https://www.gmth.de/zeitschrift/artikel/1132.aspx

cues.title: The footsteps outlast the voice
cues.text: After a slight slowing, a tempo brings back the walking pace. The final sung note gives way to six bars of piano alone. The major-key goodnight has passed; the ending is minor again.
cues.evidence: OpenScore Lieder, bar 98, un poco ritard.; bar 99, a tempo and return to D minor; piano alone in bars 100–105. https://musescore.com/openscore-lieder-corpus/scores/5015378
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The singer joins the footsteps
transitions.from: Intro · Six bars of walking chords
transitions.to: A · A stranger arrives and leaves
transitions.how: Six bars of piano establish the minor-key walking chords. The singer enters with a pickup at the end of bar 7 and a descending melody. The piano keeps its quavers and its original pace beneath the new voice.
transitions.evidence: OpenScore Lieder, bars 1–14, original D-minor edition. https://musescore.com/openscore-lieder-corpus/scores/5015378

transitions.title: The third verse follows the first
transitions.from: A · A stranger arrives and leaves
transitions.to: B · Love wanders from one to another
transitions.how: Five bars of piano lead to the third verse over the same minor-key walking chords. Duhan omits the repeat that would carry the second stanza, moving directly from remembered love to the question of why he should stay.
transitions.evidence: Utz, ZGMTH 18 (2021), footnote 25, on Duhan’s omission of the second stanza: https://www.gmth.de/zeitschrift/artikel/1132.aspx. OpenScore Lieder, bars 34–39: https://musescore.com/openscore-lieder-corpus/scores/5015378.

transitions.title: The same steps in major
transitions.from: B · Love wanders from one to another
transitions.to: C · A quiet goodnight in the major
transitions.how: The piano plays five bars alone, then the last stanza begins pianissimo in the major. Schubert changes D minor to D major, raising F to F♯. The quaver chords keep their pace while the singer tries to leave without waking his beloved.
transitions.evidence: OpenScore Lieder, bars 66–71, D-major signature and pp at bar 71; Müller, final stanza. https://musescore.com/openscore-lieder-corpus/scores/5015378; https://oxfordsong.org/song/gute-nacht

transitions.title: The minor returns beneath the farewell
transitions.from: C · A quiet goodnight in the major
transitions.to: Coda · The piano walks on in the minor
transitions.how: Un poco ritardando slows the last sung phrase. A tempo then restores the pulse and D minor returns beneath the final vocal note. The piano continues alone for six bars, ending on the minor chord.

source.title: Schubert, Winterreise No. 1, Gute Nacht, OpenScore Lieder transcription (CC0)
source.locator: Bars 1–105. Piano alone in bars 1–6, 34–38, 66–70 and 100–105. Duhan omits the second stanza, the repeat of bars 7–38 documented by Christian Utz in ZGMTH 18 (2021), footnote 25.

timeline.note: Repeated piano quavers establish the walking pace.
The voice descends over the piano’s steady chords.
Five bars of piano connect the first stanza to the third.
The singer returns with the stanza about wandering love.
The piano carries the walking chords through another interlude.
The last stanza begins softly in the major, over the same quaver steps.
The piano walks on alone and ends in the minor.

fields.label: Performers
fields.note: The label photograph of the scanned copy names Kammersänger Hans Duhan, baritone of the Vienna State Opera, with Prof. Ferdinand Foll at the piano; the Internet Archive description names the same two performers. Utz reports that Duhan recorded nineteen songs with Foll on 27 April, 2 May and 4 May 1928 and the remaining five (Nos. 16, 17, 19, 20, 23) with Lene Orthmann on 11 July 1928, so Orthmann does not play on this side. The Commons file description names only Duhan.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Abridged: the second strophe, bars 7–38 (the seconda volta), is not sung; the song runs about 4:02
fields.note: Utz lists Duhan and Foll 1928 among five early recordings that omit the second strophe, probably because the song would not otherwise fit on one side, and gives a measured length of 4:02 against a calculated 5:14 with the strophe. The key, any transposition and the absolute pitch of the transfer are not established here.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The Internet Archive description of the disc that carries this side gives the recording date. Utz lists the same three Foll session days (27 April, 2 May and 4 May 1928) without assigning songs to days, so the song-by-day assignment rests on the Internet Archive uploader’s labelling. Commons gives only the year 1928.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: No source consulted names the studio or city of the session.

fields.label: Label
fields.value: His Master’s Voice, as printed on the scanned copy (manufactured by The Gramophone Company (Czechoslovakia) Limited, Ústí nad Labem)
fields.note: The label photograph of this scanned copy shows the His Master’s Voice imprint; the photographed copies of the later discs (3, 6, 12) carry Gramola Record labels, so the photographed copies of this set carry both imprints. The label gives no date, and nothing here dates the first issue or shows that the audio transfer derives from the photographed copy.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The label photograph of the scanned copy prints Cat. No. ES 383, and the Commons file name and the Internet Archive description agree.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: CK 2946, take 2 (run-out “Ck 2946” with II); side No. 1 (label number 0942026); reverse side: Die Wetterfahne (matrix CK 2947-2). Disc 1 of 12 of the set; 30 cm.
fields.note: The label photograph of the scanned copy shows the matrix and take in the run-out; the Internet Archive description and the Commons file name give the same matrix and take. The set was issued as twelve discs, one song to a side (Utz). The photograph is of one copy and does not identify the copy from which the audio was transferred.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: No transfer engineer is named. The Commons file was uploaded on 11 August 2015 by the user Patachonf and re-uploaded on 10 and 15 February 2022 by the user Mitar; the Internet Archive item was added on 25 April 2019 by the uploader recordplayer78. These are upload facts, not transfer credits.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: No transfer date is identified. Upload dates are not treated as transfer dates.

fields.label: Processing
fields.note: Both hosts hold a FLAC file. The Commons duration (249.00 s) and the Internet Archive FLAC length (248.85 s) agree within 0.15 s, which suggests the same digitisation; which host received it first is not established, and the source disc, stylus, equalisation and noise treatment are undocumented.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Both the music and the poem are out of copyright where the ordinary life-plus-70 term applies.
fields.note: Schubert died in 1828 and the poet Wilhelm Müller in 1827. This is a term calculation, not a worldwide clearance or a statement about any modern edition.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3 — territorial: sound recording public domain in the European Union (pre-1963 publication basis).
fields.note: Commons applies PD-EU-audio to this recording, attributed to 1928. The Internet Archive item carries a Creative Commons Public Domain Mark 1.0 licence URL, which is the uploader’s assertion and is not treated as authority to waive any rights. The publication date of the original disc is not documented; the EU basis here depends on the recording being first published before 1963, which is inferred from its 1928 session. Not established as public domain in the United States.
alts: PD-EU-audio — European performers’ and producers’ rights claimed expired.
Public Domain Mark 1.0 — licence URL on the Internet Archive item, uploader’s assertion.

composer.epithet: At seventeen he set a spinning wheel turning under Gretchen’s voice; at thirty-one he could make two cellos sing as if they had always belonged together.
facts: Vienna Stadtkonvikt, 1808–13; composition lessons with Antonio Salieri
School assistant; tutor to the Esterházy daughters at Zseliz in 1818 and 1824; independent composer
The singer Vogl, the poets Schober and Mayrhofer, the painter Schwind, Josef von Spaun
More than 600 songs; symphonies, chamber music, piano sonatas and duets, masses and stage works

quote.text: I like these songs more than all the others, and you will come to like them too.
quote.source: Schubert to his friends about Winterreise, 1827, as Josef von Spaun later recalled; our translation

composer.background:
In the Schubert family quartet, Franz played the viola. His brothers took the violins and his father the cello: the future songwriter learnt to make himself heard from an inner part. He was born on 31 January 1797 in Himmelpfortgrund, a Viennese suburb, and grew up in his father’s schoolhouse. His father taught him violin, his brother Ignaz piano, and the parish musician Michael Holzer helped with the rest. At eleven he entered the imperial chapel choir and the Stadtkonvikt boarding school, where the orchestra put Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven under his fingers.

Salieri began teaching him composition in 1812. The next year Schubert left the boarding school, trained as a teacher and returned to his father’s classroom as an assistant. On 19 October 1814, aged seventeen, he wrote Gretchen am Spinnrade. The piano’s right hand turns the wheel, the left hand works the treadle, and Goethe’s girl cannot stop thinking about Faust. At the remembered kiss the mechanism stops. The following year brought roughly 140 songs, among them Erlkönig, as well as church music, a symphony and works for the stage.
